findings.message: Priority 8 recommendation to 'audit the metadata present on each of the 5 audited pages and identify which expected fields are absent' names neither the specific missing fields nor the specific pages where they are absent. The follow-on bullet to 'ensure that Open Graph and any other social or agent-facing metadata fields are consistently populated' adds a domain name (Open Graph) but no data anchor — no field name, no page URL, no count of missing fields drawn from the audit. The entire priority block contains only the aggregate score (51/100) as a data anchor; no specific missing field is identified. A recommendation to populate 'Open Graph and any other social or agent-facing metadata fields' could be pasted verbatim into any web audit for any site.
findings.context: **Priority 8: Metadata Stack Completeness 51/100** [...] Audit the metadata present on each of the 5 audited pages and identify which expected fields are absent [...] Ensure that Open Graph and any other social or agent-facing metadata fields are consistently populated across the audited set.

findings.message: 'Leaves something to be desired' equivalent: the phrase 'the heading structure across the audited set is inconsistent or incomplete in ways that reduce the clarity of the content hierarchy for search crawlers' is passive-aggressive softening that condemns without naming a specific deficiency. It conveys that the headings fall short of an implied standard without stating what is actually wrong, which is the functional equivalent of 'could be improved significantly'.
findings.context: **Priority 6: SEO 73/100 — Heading Quality 61/100** [...] heading quality sits at 61/100, indicating that the heading structure across the audited set is inconsistent or incomplete in ways that reduce the clarity of the content hierarchy for search crawlers.

findings.message: The Error Page Test table contains two cells with bracketed placeholder text that were never resolved with real audit data: 'Custom error page: [Yes: branded page with navigation / No: generic server error]' and 'Navigation back to valid content: [Yes: home link, sitemap / No]' and 'Internal navigation links: [N: links to same-site pages / None: no links to valid content]'. These are unfilled template slots — the square-bracket alternatives were options for the report generator to choose between, not client-facing prose. A client reading this table sees the internal template machinery rather than a completed audit result.
findings.context: ## Error Page Test [...] | Custom error page | [Yes: branded page with navigation / No: generic server error] | [...] | Navigation back to valid content | [Yes: home link, sitemap / No] | [...] | Internal navigation links | [N: links to same-site pages / None: no links to valid content] |

findings.message: The Appendix B Link Inventory states 'We recorded every internal link found on every audited page: [N] links in total.' The placeholder '[N]' was never substituted with the actual count from the audit data. The table immediately below supplies the per-class breakdown (733 same-host internal links, etc.), so the total is derivable, but the unreplaced '[N]' token is a leaked template placeholder visible to the client.
findings.context:
## Appendix B: Link Inventory

We recorded every internal link found on every audited page: [N] links in total.

findings.message: American English spelling 'Optimization' appears in the 'Full Optimization' phase label inside the Next Steps table. The report otherwise uses British forms throughout (e.g. 'optimisation' in the scoring methodology section and 'organise' equivalents elsewhere). This is a US/UK register inconsistency within the same document.
findings.context: ## Next Steps [...] | Full Optimization | P1, P2, P3, P4, P5, P6, P7, P8, P9 (P1–P9) | Full machine readiness — every agent, search engine, and structured-data consumer can read, trust, and act on the site |
